agent.name: Emerging Technology Diffusion Agent
agent.specialty: Rogers diffusion, application and peer diffusion, and bounded organizational timing

analytical_question: For LLM-based generative AI used for human-reviewed code suggestions, explanations, test drafts and bounded refactoring, what evidence distinguishes individual developer use, recurring application use and sustained firm-level deployment among comparable mid-sized software engineering organizations, and what conditional evaluation-versus-standardization timing follows for a hypothetical fast-follower firm over a relative six-month horizon? Its geography, local adoption baseline and actual test execution date are unknown.
general_et_finding: As of the closed diffusion-v0.2 evidence snapshot prepared 2026-11-01 America/New_York (not an execution date), surveyed technology workers show substantial broad-AI use, beyond access alone. E1-C1 reports 90% current workplace AI use among surveyed technology professionals in 2025, and E1-C2 reports that 60% of surveyed AI users used AI about half the time or more when encountering a task/problem during the prior three months. E4-C1 reports 75.9% relying at least partly on AI for one or more daily professional responsibilities in its 2024 respondent group. These are individual self-reports with distinct denominators and broad AI wording, not LLM-only, daily-active telemetry, longitudinal persistence, authorized firm deployment, world prevalence or a measured adoption curve. D1-D3 show issuer-described availability and ecosystems, not prevalence. Relative to the social system of surveyed technical workers, use appears widespread within these samples, but population timing and sampling evidence cannot identify an exact Rogers stage. Innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards classify relative adoption timing within a defined social system; their theoretical proportions are not survey prevalence thresholds. Global LLM diffusion, saturation, S-curve shape and a 2026 adopter-category distribution remain unresolved. Fieldwork endpoints for E1/E4 are not reported in supplied evidence, and the historic observations require refreshing under the 12-month review policy; the actual ChatGPT execution date is not supplied and must not be inferred from preparation or retrieval timestamps.
application_finding: Application boundary: assisted software development with human-reviewed suggestions, explanations, test drafts and bounded refactoring, not autonomous engineering. E4-C2 reports 74.9% partial AI reliance among 2024 respondents whose work included writing code; it is individual task reliance, not LLM-only firm deployment. E2-C2 measures respondents’ estimates of AI-supported team work over the preceding three months, not audited institutional penetration. No dated denominator of comparable mid-sized software firms, authorized routine coding-assistant deployments, paid seats or sustained cohort retention is supplied; peer diffusion stage and majority-firm claims are unknown. Five Rogers characteristics: Relative advantage — observation: E4 coding-task reliance and E2 observational study of incorporation, but no directly verified quality-adjusted time saving or causal productivity effect; effect mixed/possible accelerator through faster drafting versus review, defects and rework; condition: measure task-level quality, cycle time, security and rework against baseline; confidence low in net advantage. Compatibility — observation: D2 issuer-described VS Code suggestions/chat and enterprise-admin channel; likely accelerator for supported editors, potentially inhibitor for restricted repositories, policies or workflow mismatch; condition: validate this firm’s repositories, IDEs, IP/data rules and approvals; confidence moderate in described integration, low in local fit. Complexity — observation: D2 documents version/model-update dependencies; E3 participants describe code verification and skill-protection practices in a student setting; mixed effect as familiar interfaces may lower entry costs but prompting, verification, updates, training and CI integration add work; condition: test training/support demand and reviewer workload; confidence moderate in documented dependencies, low in company-wide burden. Trialability — observation: D2 describes free sign-up and enterprise-admin access, and D1 describes historical general availability; likely accelerator if a permissioned, reversible pilot can isolate code/data and measure outcomes, but approvals and setup are costs; condition: security-approved scope, rollback and representative task set; confidence moderate in access descriptions and low in actual local feasibility. Observability — observation: no direct measured peer outcome evidence; mixed/unknown because demos and visible generated code may spread awareness while trustworthy speed, defect and rework outcomes require independent comparison; condition: shared outcome definitions and reproducible peer/local measurements; confidence low. Mechanisms: D1/D2 show a GitHub/Microsoft distribution and IDE ecosystem (not independent adoption replications), potentially amplifying access through product channels; D2 update/admin dependencies may impede compatibility. Candidate internal change agents are engineering enablement and security leaders, and potential opinion leaders are respected senior developers, but no actual endorsements or peer-network effects are observed. Peer talks, technical communities and vendor materials are possible communication channels, not verified causal accelerators. Existing review/CI, training, governance and repository controls are hypothesized complementary assets or barriers; no universal interoperability standard or measured diffusion effect is established. E3 provides bounded student qualitative support for trust, verification and skill concerns rather than a professional prevalence estimate.
organization_specific_finding: The mid-sized software company and its existing repositories, review/CI, finite integration capacity and pilot capability are hypothetical scenario assumptions, not observed facts. “Fast Follower” describes management’s intention to learn from comparable peers before broad standardization; it is not a formal Rogers category or evidence that the organization is early majority. Its own adopter category and relative rank among similar firms cannot be assigned without dated peer timing, firm-level usage definitions and a local baseline. Compared with an aggressive startup, a peer-evidence gate is more valuable under the specified posture; compared with clinical documentation, coding tasks permit a narrower human-reviewed evaluation under assumed existing engineering checks, though faulty or insecure code, disclosure and customer impacts remain consequential. Conditional timing: establish authorized use and baseline immediately, then consider a reversible repository/task-bounded pilot within the relative six-month horizon, with a near-term review after a proposed 4–8 week measurement window. Standardization should depend on repeatable quality-adjusted outcomes, retained use, security approval and relevant peer evidence; weak results, unsafe code or data-handling gaps justify delay or rollback. Actual run date and calendar horizon endpoints are unknown.

evidence.claim: E1-C1: 90% of surveyed technology professionals report current AI use at work; individual current use, not LLM-only or firm-level deployment.
evidence.date_or_recency: 2025 publication; 2025 survey; exact fieldwork dates not reported in supplied evidence; snapshot prepared 2026-11-01.
evidence.evidence_type: Original DORA/Google Cloud cross-sectional survey infographic and inspected questionnaire.
evidence.notes: Nearly 5,000 technology professionals worldwide; exact item n, country weighting, recruitment and probability sampling design not reported in supplied evidence. Representativeness is not established, and design must not be asserted nonprobability. Google Cloud affiliation; broad AI-tools wording; self-reported use; historical by snapshot.

evidence.claim: E1-C2: 60% of surveyed AI users report using AI about half the time or more on encountered tasks/problems over the last three months; individual retrospective frequency.
evidence.date_or_recency: 2025 survey/report; three-month recall item; exact fieldwork period not reported in supplied evidence.
evidence.evidence_type: Original issuer survey summary and original instrument.
evidence.notes: Denominator is surveyed AI users, not all technology professionals, firms or daily-active users; item n and E1 sampling design unknown. Does not show cohort persistence or authorized enterprise rollout.

evidence.claim: E2-C1/E2-C2/E2-C3: Rounded 76% AI reliance repeats E4 2024 data; team incorporation is respondents’ estimate of AI-supported work in preceding three months; license/DAU telemetry is measurement advice.
evidence.date_or_recency: March 2025 release; evidence from 2024 survey and September 2024 interviews, not a new 2025 prevalence wave.
evidence.evidence_type: DORA/Google Cloud observational survey analysis, Bayesian modeling, and qualitative interviews.
evidence.notes: Underlying 2024 respondent group and 10 roughly 90-minute development-professional interviews; percentages of team work are not percentages of adopting organizations. E2 and E4 are dependent; no randomized causal productivity effect or collected local DAU data.

evidence.claim: E3-C1: Student participants describe moderating AI, checking generated code, and protecting skill development; possible verification and trust mechanisms.
evidence.date_or_recency: Published/updated 2026-02-17; eight-month study with calendar fieldwork dates not reported in supplied evidence.
evidence.notes: UC Berkeley EECS, design and data-science students; participant n and sampling frame not reported. Not an estimate of professional use prevalence, organization adoption or causal impact.

evidence.claim: E4-C1/E4-C2: 75.9% of 2024 DORA respondents relied partly on AI for a daily professional responsibility; 74.9% of respondents with coding responsibilities relied partly on AI for writing code.
evidence.date_or_recency: 2024 report and survey; precise fieldwork and release day not reported in supplied evidence; older than 12-month review flag.
evidence.evidence_type: Original DORA/Google Cloud self-report survey and inspected methods.
evidence.notes: Nearly 3,000 respondents across 104 countries overall, not necessarily every item. E4 documents organic blog/email/social/snowball plus supplementary-panel recruitment and three randomized survey flows (not treatment assignment). E4-specific self-selection/method limitations cannot be transferred to E1. Item-level n unavailable; neither rate is LLM-only or firm penetration.

evidence.claim: D1: Historical Copilot technical-preview repository states general availability; technical access channel only.
evidence.date_or_recency: Undated archived README, retrieved 2026-11-02T00:51:23.545126+00:00; linked announcement URL dated 2022-06-21 was not independently retrieved.
evidence.notes: No user denominator, adoption observation, sustained-use metric or impact study. Availability as a potential trialability mechanism is inference. Corporate ecosystem overlap with D2.

evidence.claim: D2: Archived VS Code Copilot Chat README describes inline suggestions, chat, agents, free sign-up, enterprise-admin access and version/update dependencies.
evidence.notes: Issuer claims about product integration, not validated current entitlements, usage or effectiveness. Possible compatibility, complexity and access mechanisms are analyst inference; not independent of D1 ecosystem.

evidence.claim: D3: MedGemma README describes medical model variants, notebooks and access links, not clinical-documentation deployment.
evidence.evidence_type: Original Google Health model repository README.
evidence.notes: No hospital or clinician denominator, ambient-scribe use, independent clinical efficacy or authorization. Relevant only to weak-claim boundary; existence of ecosystem does not equal documentation diffusion.

contrary_evidence_or_limitations: High self-reported AI use among technical respondents coexists with absent LLM-only denominators, firm-level authorized deployment counts, repeated retention telemetry and firm-peer sampling; the gap prevents a majority-firm or exact stage conclusion, not a conclusion of nonuse.

E1 2025 recruitment/probability sampling design, weighting, per-item n and fieldwork dates are not reported in supplied evidence. Neither representative nor nonprobability status can be asserted; E4’s documented recruitment limitations apply to E4 only.

E4 2024 data and E1 2025 observations trigger the policy refresh flag by November 2026. E2 repeats E4 rather than independently confirming growth. E3 student qualitative material cannot refresh professional prevalence. No subtraction of 75.9% and 90% is a valid growth estimate.

D1/D2 technical availability, free access and vendor integration are not observed active use or productivity; E2 associations are not experimental causal effects. Code output may impose testing, verification, rework or security costs.

The claim “most comparable hospitals now routinely use LLM-assisted clinical documentation” is unsupported: technical-worker measures and a medical-model README contain no hospital documentation denominator or sustained-use measure; absence of evidence is not proof of hospital nonuse.

Comparable firm geography, local policies and actual use, peer timing, outcome baselines, full survey methods and execution date are unspecified. Direct blocked external leads were not inspected and provide no admitted evidence.
confidence_and_uncertainty: Moderate confidence that the original DORA documents report substantial broad-AI current and recurring individual use among sampled technology workers, and that a 2024 coding-responsibility subset reported substantial partial task reliance. Low confidence in precise current LLM-only population penetration or a Rogers category: E1 representativeness is unestablished because its sampling design is unknown, E4 has documented selection limits, sources share issuer affiliation, and observation periods are historical. Low confidence in routine deployment or peer rank among comparable mid-sized software firms because no institution denominator, geography, workflow-defined active use or longitudinal observations are available. Low conditional confidence in this hypothetical firm’s timing until local governance, baseline, task quality and peer measures are collected. Evidence snapshot preparation and README retrieval dates are not actual test execution dates; actual execution date is unknown, so the six-month horizon has no supplied calendar endpoints.
value_opportunity_implication: Potential benefits include faster human-reviewed code explanations, suggestions, tests and bounded refactoring and more systematic developer learning. E4’s task reliance demonstrates reported use, not net benefit. Test whether any cycle-time improvements survive quality, rework, training, licensing and review costs for this firm; do not assign an unsupported ROI or uplift.
risk_governance_implication: Keep developers and accountable reviewers responsible for code, tests, merge approvals and production effects. Before evaluation, confirm repository confidentiality/IP rules, tool data flows and retention, access and security controls, approval ownership and incident/rollback procedures. CI and code review are assumed assets, not proof of secure output. Security or legal approval is not certified by this diffusion analysis.
recommendation_management_implication: Timing guidance only: first have engineering management and security identify actual existing access/use, candidate tasks, local baseline, peer comparison criteria and an accountable pilot owner. If governance permits, run a reversible, bounded coding-assistant comparison with human review and proposed 4–8 week check-in inside the relative six-month horizon. Record meaningful weekly use, repeated use, quality-adjusted throughput, defects/rework, disclosure incidents and training burden against controls or baseline; seek dated comparable-firm data. Consider later standardization only after stable benefits and safety/governance gates are met. Delay or reverse on adverse quality/security findings, inability to protect code, poor retention or unresolvable comparator gaps. Full adoption authorization remains with the Adoption Agent and accountable management.
change_monitoring_triggers: Engineering enablement owner candidate: define eligible developers, approved access, trial starts, meaningful weekly active use, repeat-cohort retention, task mix and support demand; review after a proposed 4–8 weeks, not as a documented commitment.

Engineering quality and security owners: compare reviewed defect/rework rates, CI outcomes, task cycle time, sensitive-data handling and incidents against the pre-pilot baseline; pause if management-defined safety conditions fail.

Research/strategy owner candidate: refresh 2024/2025 survey observations with dated original LLM-specific developer and firm-level data, including sampling frame, field dates, geography, item denominators, organizational authorization and ongoing use.
Engineering leadership: obtain comparable mid-sized firms’ time-stamped organization-level routine-use definitions and deployment duration; re-evaluate peer-position claims when credible data arrive.

Accountable decision owner to be designated: revisit evaluation-to-standardization gate at completion of the proposed pilot or upon a material tooling, policy, quality or security change, within the relative six-month planning horizon.
abstention_or_more_information_needed: Abstain from a numerical 2026 LLM-only penetration rate, worldwide Rogers category, S-curve or forecast date: obtain dated, application-specific surveys with defined social system, geography, recruitment/sampling design, per-item denominators, fieldwork dates and repeated-use measures.

Abstain from “most comparable software firms routinely deploy LLM coding assistants” and this company’s Rogers category/peer rank: obtain a comparable-firm organizational sampling frame, defined authorized production use, active-team and seat denominators, deployment dates, repeat telemetry and the company’s local baseline.

Abstain from “most comparable hospitals now routinely use LLM-assisted clinical documentation”: obtain original dated hospital-level survey/administrative evidence defining geography, specialty, institution denominator, routine documentation workflow, sampling frame, fieldwork and sustained adoption; D3 cannot substitute.
Abstain from a causal productivity gain or expected ROI: collect quality-adjusted task outcomes, review time, defects, rework, tool/training costs and a suitable comparative evaluation.

Request firm geography, current permitted use, tools, repository/data controls, budget, accountable decision owner and pilot eligibility. The actual test execution date was not explicitly supplied; do not infer it from evidence dates, and express the planning horizon as six relative months.
